text:
🇮🇳🇺🇸 X TO INDIA: WE’RE NOT DONE FIGHTING FOR FREE SPEECH

X says India’s new takedown rules have “no basis in law” and violate free expression.

A court just tossed X’s legal challenge, but the platform’s appealing - and calling the system censorship.

One judge ruled that “liberty is yoked with responsibility,” saying platforms must follow Indian laws if they want to operate there.

X says it respects the law but still has the right to speak up:

“X is deeply concerned by the recent order from the Karnataka court in India, which will allow millions of police officers to issue arbitrary takedown orders through a secretive online portal called the Sahyog. 

This new regime has no basis in the law, circumvents Section 69A of the IT Act, violates Supreme Court rulings, and infringes Indian citizens’ constitutional rights to freedom of speech and expression. 

The Sahyog enables officers to order content removal based solely on allegations of “illegality,” without judicial review or due process for the speakers, and threatens platforms with criminal liability for non-compliance.

X respects and complies with Indian law, but this order fails to address the core constitutional issues in our challenge and is inconsistent with the Bombay High Court's recent ruling that a similar regime was unconstitutional. 

We respectfully disagree with the view that we have no right to raise these concerns because of our incorporation abroad—X contributes significantly to public discourse in India and the voice of our users is at the heart of our platform. 

We will appeal this order to defend free expression.”

Source: Reuters, @GlobalAffairs

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

@SFLCin has received a response to its RTI application DITEC/R/E/25/00263 on the total number of URLs blocked by MeitY from 2010 to 2024. The URLs include social media accounts, channels, webpages, websites, pages etc on various social media platforms.

Number of URLs blocked under Section 69A are 362, 62, 471, 500, 633, 1385, 2799, 3635, 9849, 6096, ,6775 and 12483 and 12863 during the year 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024 respectively.

The data indicates a rising trend in the issuance of blocking orders by MeitY, particularly in 2023 and 2024, coinciding with the Farmers’ Protest and General Election 2024.

@GoI_MeitY is empowered to issue blocking directions under Section 69A of The Information Technology Act, 2000. Rule 16 of the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009 also facilitates blanket confidentiality regarding the requests, complaints, and actions taken for blocking information. This rule enables the authorities to block access to content without providing a reasoned order or issuing any notice to the originator of the content due to which details regarding the URLs blocked are not available in the public domain. 

Earlier this month, the Supreme Court issued a notice on @SFLCin's legal challenge to Rule 16 of the Information Technology Blocking Rules of 2009.

In her video, she says she cannot go LIVE for a year, send messages, post videos to her broadcast group or share videos to her Story. She also describes monetisation being unavailable and some content becoming inaccessible in India.

She says she had made a video supporting Neha Singh Rathore and opposing ABVP-related groups. According to her account, she was not clearly informed which specific post had triggered the restrictions and had to investigate the matter herself.

These are the creator’s allegations and account of her experience. The precise reason for the restrictions, the applicable Meta policy and whether a government direction was involved have not been independently established from this video alone.

But her experience raises a fundamental democratic question: What happens when ordinary citizens and independent creators lose their ability to communicate with their audiences without receiving a clear explanation?

THIS IS NOT AN ISOLATED CONCERN

Recent reporting in India makes these questions particularly urgent.

• ThePrint, 19 October 2026: Reported on a MeitY advisory asking Meta to review its Facebook and Instagram recommendation systems, alongside restrictions affecting posts and accounts connected with protests and political events.

https://t.co/QeWUIIrGmC

• Alt News, 15 October 2026: Documented restrictions affecting journalists and media organisations covering the Delhi protests, including cases in which Meta notices cited automated enforcement or government and law-enforcement requests.

https://t.co/1RjkoJX1nE

• Reporters Without Borders: Reported a broader rise in restrictions affecting journalistic content in India during 2026, raising concerns about opaque takedown processes and the public’s right to information.

https://t.co/g6FhmAUglC

These reports provide important context. They do not, by themselves, establish that this particular creator was restricted at the government's request. That question deserves a direct, evidence-based answer.

THE REAL ISSUE: TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY

Social media companies have the right to enforce legitimate community standards. But enforcement must be proportionate, transparent and open to meaningful appeal.

If a creator is prohibited from going LIVE for an entire year, the platform should explain:

Which specific post, video or action triggered the restriction?
Which rule was allegedly violated, and what evidence supports that decision?
Was the action taken under Meta's own policies, an automated system or a government/legal request?
Why were such extensive restrictions imposed, and what appeal and restoration mechanisms are available?

A vague account-status notification is not an adequate substitute for a meaningful explanation.

DEMOCRACY CANNOT BE MEASURED ONLY BY ELECTIONS

Democracy also depends on the freedom to question power, criticise political organisations, support dissenting voices and share information without arbitrary punishment.

When restrictions disproportionately affect people discussing political controversies, the public deserves to know whether the cause is legitimate policy enforcement, automated error, coordinated reporting or an external legal direction. These possibilities must be investigated rather than assumed.

Our demand is simple: transparency from Meta, accountability from any authority that seeks unlawful restrictions, and equal protection for every citizen's right to express a political opinion.

No creator should have to guess why their voice has been restricted. No government should be allowed to silence lawful criticism through opaque processes. And no technology company should be permitted to hide consequential decisions behind unexplained notifications.

If the restrictions were justified, publish the reasons. If they were mistaken or unlawful, restore the affected rights. Let evidence decide—not political loyalty.

Every week someone tells me they vibe-coded their app over the weekend and don't need developers anymore.

Before it touches a paying customer, make sure it includes:

> a schema someone designed, instead of one the AI improvised table by table
> login that still works when someone puts a plus sign in their email
> password reset links that expire and work once
> MFA, plus a recovery path for the user who lost their phone
> sessions that time out, and a way to kill every session for one user
> SSO for the enterprise customer who won't sign without it
> SAML, because that customer's IT team doesn't do magic links
> SCIM, so a fired employee loses access the moment IT offboards them
> roles and permissions deeper than "admin" and "everyone else"
> checks that stop user A from reading user B's data by changing one number in the URL
> tenant isolation, so one customer's bug never shows another customer's records
> an admin "log in as this user" button for support, with an audit trail on every use
> rate limits on login, so nobody can guess passwords at scale
> lockouts that stop attackers without locking out your CFO the night before the board meeting
> database migrations that run forward and roll back
> migrations that don't lock the main table at 2pm on a Tuesday
> indexes, because the query that was instant on 50 test rows times out on 5 million real ones
> connection pooling, so a traffic spike doesn't exhaust the database
> backups every night
> a restore from those backups, tested, because a backup you've never restored is a hope
> point-in-time recovery for the day someone runs a delete without a where clause
> soft deletes, so "I deleted it by accident" is a support ticket and not an incident
> validation on the server, not just in the form
> timezones stored right, so the 9am reminder doesn't fire at 4am
> the customer with an apostrophe in their last name
> emoji, accents and right-to-left text in every field
> money stored as integers, because 0.1 + 0.2 doesn't equal 0.3 in floating point
> currency, rounding and tax rules for every country you sell into
> a data model that survives your second customer asking for "one small change"
> idempotency keys, so a retried payment doesn't charge the card twice
> deduplication for the user who clicks submit four times
> pagination that still works on page 400
> exports, because sooner or later every customer wants their data in a spreadsheet
> imports that survive the CSV someone saved in 2009
> retention rules, and code that deletes what your contract says you'll delete
> secrets out of the code, out of the repo and out of the AI chat history
> rotating every key the AI pasted into a config file last month
> confirming every package the AI installed exists and is the one you meant
> dependency scanning, because the AI pulled in libraries nobody reviewed
> input sanitization everywhere a user can type
> protection against SQL injection, XSS, CSRF and the rest of the OWASP list
> file uploads that get scanned, size-limited and stored where they can't execute
> CORS rules that aren't "allow everything"
> security headers on every response
> encryption at rest and in transit
> least-privilege access for everyone, including the AI agent holding production credentials
> logs that record who did what, without recording passwords, tokens or card numbers
> a penetration test before your enterprise customer's security team runs their own
> answers to the security questionnaire every enterprise buyer sends, with evidence behind each one
> a disclosure process for the day a stranger emails you a vulnerability
> a plan for the day a laptop with production access gets stolen
> SOC 2, which means policies, evidence and an auditor, not a checkbox
> HIPAA, the moment a single patient record touches your system
> a BAA with every vendor that touches that data, including your AI model provider
> audit trails that show who viewed a record, not just who changed it
> PCI scope, and card numbers kept out of your database
> GDPR deletion requests that reach every table, backup and log
> data residency for the customer whose contract says EU only
> quarterly access reviews someone signs off on
> dev, staging and production environments that match each other
> infrastructure written as code, so the setup lives somewhere other than one person's memory
> a deploy pipeline that runs the tests before anything reaches customers
> one-click rollbacks, because Friday deploys happen
> zero-downtime deploys, because your customers don't have maintenance windows
> feature flags, so you can ship the code without shipping the feature
> autoscaling for the Monday morning spike
> a CDN, so the app loads fast in Singapore too
> DNS, SSL certificates, and renewals that don't expire on a Sunday
> background job queues, so slow work doesn't freeze the page
> retries with backoff, so one flaky API call doesn't become a lost order
> a dead-letter queue for the jobs that fail every retry
> cron jobs that don't run twice the day you add a second server
> caching, and clearing that cache when the data changes
> SPF, DKIM and DMARC, so your password resets don't land in spam
> bounce and complaint handling on every transactional email
> storage rules, so you stop paying to keep 2021's temp files
> cost alerts, so a runaway agent loop shows up the same day and not on the invoice (we learned this one for $1,382.59)
> a disaster recovery plan, written down and tested once a year
> a second region, if your contract promises uptime one region can't deliver
> structured logs you can search at 3am
> error tracking that groups the same bug instead of sending you 4,000 emails
> uptime checks from outside your own network
> alerts that page a human, tuned until they stop paging for nothing
> dashboards for latency, error rate and throughput
> tracing for one slow request across every service it touches
> an on-call rotation, and a person who picks up
> runbooks, so the engineer on call knows what "queue depth critical" means
> postmortems that change something
> a status page customers check before they email you
> unit tests written by someone who knows what the logic should do
> integration tests for every third-party API you depend on
> end-to-end tests for signup, checkout and the other flows that make you money
> load testing before the launch email goes out
> test data that looks like production without being production data
> regression tests, so fixing bug 41 doesn't bring back bug 12
> testing on the five-year-old laptop your biggest customer's ops team still uses
> accessibility compliance, because the enterprise contract requires it
> subscriptions, upgrades, downgrades and proration
> failed-payment retries and dunning emails
> invoices with the customer's PO number on them, because procurement won't pay without it
> sales tax and VAT
> refunds, credits and partial refunds
> usage metering that matches what you bill, to the cent
> annual contracts with custom terms your billing logic never planned for
> revenue reports your finance team can reconcile
> webhooks that verify signatures
> webhooks that retry, with a log of every failed delivery
> a versioned API, so you can change it without breaking your customers' integrations
> API keys customers can create and revoke
> API rate limits that protect you without blocking real integrations
> a plan for the day a third-party API changes its response format without telling you
> OAuth token refresh, because tokens expire at the worst possible moment
> a sandbox where customers can test their integration
> protection against prompt injection in every field that reaches the model
> customer and patient data kept out of prompts that leave your network
> a model spend cap per customer, so one heavy user can't run up your bill
> evals, so you find out when a model update makes your answers worse
> a fallback for the afternoon your model provider goes down
> a migration plan for the day your model gets deprecated
> prompt and output logs for debugging, minus whatever you're not allowed to keep
> a human approval step for anything the AI does that can't be undone
> pages that load on hotel wifi
> empty states, loading states and error states on every screen
> error messages a customer can act on, instead of "something went wrong"
> forms that keep what people typed when one field fails validation
> emails that render in every mail client your customers use
> notifications people can turn off
> undo
> keyboard navigation and screen reader support
> translations, with dates and numbers formatted for each locale
> a back button that does what people expect
> code a human can read
> code review on every change
> a branching strategy, so two people can work without overwriting each other
> monthly dependency upgrades, so you're never two major versions behind
> framework upgrades before the old version stops getting security patches
> deleting the dead code the AI left behind from its first three attempts
> splitting up the 2,000-line file the AI kept appending to
> architecture decisions written down, with the reasons
> a README that gets a new engineer running locally in under an hour
> documentation for whoever inherits this
> an admin panel for your ops team
> support tooling, so customer success can answer questions without pinging engineering
> a changelog customers can read
> terms and a privacy policy that match what the code does
> every account, domain and repo in the company's name, not the name of whoever built the prototype
> a bus factor higher than one

Oh, and besides keeping all of this working every day, forever… your vibe-coded app will still need people who know what they're doing:

> reading every line the AI wrote before it ships (a senior engineer)
> designing the data model before your second customer breaks it (a backend engineer)
> explaining why the AI's fix for one bug created two new ones (a senior engineer, again)
> deploys, rollbacks, servers and the cloud bill (a DevOps engineer)
> answering the page at 3am when payments stop (whoever's on call)
> patching the framework the week a vulnerability goes public (security)
> walking an auditor through how patient data moves (security and compliance)
> testing what the AI says it tested (QA)
> running a migration on a live database without losing a row (a backend engineer)
> saying no to the feature that breaks three others (a tech lead)
> turning "works on my laptop" into "works for every customer at once" (an architect)
> debugging the code when the AI that wrote it can't (a senior engineer)
> remembering why it's built this way, a year from now (someone who was there)

…wishing them the best 🫡

Every Indian needs to know about this because it is a massive deal for how we trust anything on the internet.

Let me explain.

When you open your bank's website, there's a small padlock next to the web address. That padlock means two things. 

First, that you're talking to your real bank. 

And second that nobody can read what you type, like your password.

So how does your browser know the website is real?

It checks the website's certificate. Think of it like an ID card for a website. 

Your Aadhaar is trusted because the government issued it. A website's ID card is trusted because a certificate authority issued it.

A certificate authority, or CA, is a company that browsers like Chrome, Firefox and Safari already trust. If a CA says "yes, this really is this bank's website," your browser believes it and shows the padlock.

eMudhra is an Indian CA. It's a big one, with more than 60 million certificates issued over the years.

So how does a CA sign these ID cards?

Every CA has a secret number called a private key. It uses that number to put a stamp on each certificate. 

Your browser checks the stamp to confirm it really came from that CA.

The whole system only works if that number is impossible to guess. 

For the type of key in this story, it's supposed to be around 116 digits long. 

Every computer on Earth working together for billions of years wouldn't be able to guess a number like that, just because of the sheer combinations that exist.

But here's what happened.

On October 17, Mozilla got a report that the private keys behind eight eMudhra certificates had been compromised. 

The report came through a person called Wayne on Google's Chrome team.

The keys weren't 116 digits long. 

All eight keys were smaller than 256. Security researcher Scott Helme found that one of them was just the number 4. Others were 66, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

So anyone could break them by trying 256 numbers. A basic laptop does that in less than a second.

Mozilla didn't need to know how Wayne did it. Its own team recovered the keys within two hours. Since then, several other people have found them on their own too.

To understand the gravity of the problem, a bad actor could make fake ID cards for any website they want. 

Your bank, your email, a government portal. 

Browsers that trusted eMudhra would have checked the fake stamp and shown the padlock like everything was fine.

If someone could get between you and the internet, say on public Wi-Fi, they could show you a fake site with a real-looking padlock and read or change what you send.

eMudhra says a script used during its key creation process back in April 2025 had a flaw. It made a second, much weaker set of keys, and those were used by mistake to create the certificates.

That means these weak keys were there for about a year and a half before anyone caught it. eMudhra says the person who found it may have used AI-assisted techniques.

The good news is that the response was fast.

Mozilla received the report at 8:06 pm UTC on October 17 and had pushed a block to Firefox users by 10:59 pm.

Google, Apple and Microsoft have also blocked these certificates for their users. 

eMudhra revoked all eight the next morning and stopped issuing new certificates from the affected root. 

Mozilla is now removing that root certificate from Firefox's trusted list altogether.

But there's still a lot of clean-up to do.

Browsers are mostly covered. But plenty of apps, servers and backend systems don't check these block lists. They need software updates to stop trusting the bad certificates, and some of those updates are still pending.

Real websites that used eMudhra are also affected. Yash Kadakia, founder of Security Brigade, estimates around 30,000 legitimate certificates will need to be moved over. A lot of those are likely Indian businesses and services.

See, we're moving our whole lives online, UPI, banking, tax filing, DigiLocker, government services. 

All of it rests on this invisible layer of trust.

So, when an Indian company that's trusted by every major browser makes a mistake this basic, it hurts how the world sees Indian digital infrastructure.

This has happened before, and it went very badly. 

In 2011, a Dutch CA called DigiNotar was hacked, and fake Google certificates were used to spy on people in Iran. 

Browsers stopped trusting it completely, and the company shut down soon after.

For now, here's what you can do. Keep your browser and apps updated on your phone and laptop. 

Be careful on public Wi-Fi. Type your bank's website address yourself instead of clicking links.

eMudhra still owes India a clear, public explanation of how a key that protects millions of people ended up being the number 4.

AN APOLOGY IS NO SUBSTITUTE FOR CONSTITUTIONAL COMPLIANCE: SUPREME COURT EXPOSES EXECUTIVE OVERREACH IN DELHI INTERNET BAN

The unfolding of this episode is a telling commentary on the precarious state of our constitutional governance. That the government, faced with the judicial scrutiny of an internet ban—a measure that strikes at the very root of the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a)—has chosen to tender an unconditional apology, is a tacit admission of executive overreach.
 
However, an apology, however unconditional, cannot act as a panacea for a constitutional transgression. It is deeply concerning that an order imposing a blanket internet shutdown in the capital—crippling the flow of information and stifling dissent—was passed, seemingly without the application of mind, only to be withdrawn or apologized for once the judicial microscope was applied.
 
The Supreme Court is not merely a forum for dispute resolution; it is the ultimate sentinel on the qui vive, the guardian of the citizen's liberties against the might of the State. While the unconditional apology is noted, the Court must not allow this hasty retreat to bury the larger, grave questions of proportionality and legality under the guise of commotion.

The issuance of notice in the connected matters is a welcome step. The majesty of the Constitution demands that the executive be held accountable, for the rule of law cannot be reduced to a mere game of catch-me-if-you-can, where the State breaches fundamental rights and then seeks to absolve itself through a written apology.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

Sci-Hub is a website founded by Alexandra Elbakyan that provides free access to millions of paywalled academic papers by bypassing publisher restrictions.

The Delhi High Court ordered it blocked in India on Aug 23, 2025, following a 2020 lawsuit by publishers like Elsevier and Wiley, who claimed copyright infringement and piracy. text:
Every Indian needs to know about this because it is a massive deal for how we trust anything on the internet.

Let me explain.

When you open your bank's website, there's a small padlock next to the web address. That padlock means two things. 

First, that you're talking to your real bank. 

And second that nobody can read what you type, like your password.

So how does your browser know the website is real?

It checks the website's certificate. Think of it like an ID card for a website. 

Your Aadhaar is trusted because the government issued it. A website's ID card is trusted because a certificate authority issued it.

A certificate authority, or CA, is a company that browsers like Chrome, Firefox and Safari already trust. If a CA says "yes, this really is this bank's website," your browser believes it and shows the padlock.

eMudhra is an Indian CA. It's a big one, with more than 60 million certificates issued over the years.

So how does a CA sign these ID cards?

Every CA has a secret number called a private key. It uses that number to put a stamp on each certificate. 

Your browser checks the stamp to confirm it really came from that CA.

The whole system only works if that number is impossible to guess. 

For the type of key in this story, it's supposed to be around 116 digits long. 

Every computer on Earth working together for billions of years wouldn't be able to guess a number like that, just because of the sheer combinations that exist.

But here's what happened.

On October 17, Mozilla got a report that the private keys behind eight eMudhra certificates had been compromised. 

The report came through a person called Wayne on Google's Chrome team.

The keys weren't 116 digits long. 

All eight keys were smaller than 256. Security researcher Scott Helme found that one of them was just the number 4. Others were 66, 155, 156, 230 and 237.

So anyone could break them by trying 256 numbers. A basic laptop does that in less than a second.

Mozilla didn't need to know how Wayne did it. Its own team recovered the keys within two hours. Since then, several other people have found them on their own too.

To understand the gravity of the problem, a bad actor could make fake ID cards for any website they want. 

Your bank, your email, a government portal. 

Browsers that trusted eMudhra would have checked the fake stamp and shown the padlock like everything was fine.

If someone could get between you and the internet, say on public Wi-Fi, they could show you a fake site with a real-looking padlock and read or change what you send.

eMudhra says a script used during its key creation process back in April 2025 had a flaw. It made a second, much weaker set of keys, and those were used by mistake to create the certificates.

That means these weak keys were there for about a year and a half before anyone caught it. eMudhra says the person who found it may have used AI-assisted techniques.

The good news is that the response was fast.

Mozilla received the report at 8:06 pm UTC on October 17 and had pushed a block to Firefox users by 10:59 pm.

Google, Apple and Microsoft have also blocked these certificates for their users. 

eMudhra revoked all eight the next morning and stopped issuing new certificates from the affected root. 

Mozilla is now removing that root certificate from Firefox's trusted list altogether.

But there's still a lot of clean-up to do.

Browsers are mostly covered. But plenty of apps, servers and backend systems don't check these block lists. They need software updates to stop trusting the bad certificates, and some of those updates are still pending.

Real websites that used eMudhra are also affected. Yash Kadakia, founder of Security Brigade, estimates around 30,000 legitimate certificates will need to be moved over. A lot of those are likely Indian businesses and services.

See, we're moving our whole lives online, UPI, banking, tax filing, DigiLocker, government services. 

All of it rests on this invisible layer of trust.

So, when an Indian company that's trusted by every major browser makes a mistake this basic, it hurts how the world sees Indian digital infrastructure.

This has happened before, and it went very badly. 

In 2011, a Dutch CA called DigiNotar was hacked, and fake Google certificates were used to spy on people in Iran. 

Browsers stopped trusting it completely, and the company shut down soon after.

For now, here's what you can do. Keep your browser and apps updated on your phone and laptop. 

Be careful on public Wi-Fi. Type your bank's website address yourself instead of clicking links.

eMudhra still owes India a clear, public explanation of how a key that protects millions of people ended up being the number 4.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

Under Ohio R.C. 149.43, a requester first sends a complaint form to the clerk’s office, allowing 3 business days to cure. If unresolved, they file a mandamus action in common pleas court, appeals court, or the Supreme Court seeking an order to release the records for inspection or copies.

If the court finds noncompliance, it can compel release plus statutory damages of $100 per business day from filing (max $1,000), reasonable attorney fees in some cases, and costs. Damages come from public funds, not personal liability. 

No automatic removal or criminal penalties apply solely for this; political fallout or other existing issues for the clerk could arise separately. Records may still face lawful redactions.

Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

Every week someone tells me they vibe-coded their app over the weekend and don't need developers anymore.

Before it touches a paying customer, make sure it includes:

> a schema someone designed, instead of one the AI improvised table by table
> login that still works when someone puts a plus sign in their email
> password reset links that expire and work once
> MFA, plus a recovery path for the user who lost their phone
> sessions that time out, and a way to kill every session for one user
> SSO for the enterprise customer who won't sign without it
> SAML, because that customer's IT team doesn't do magic links
> SCIM, so a fired employee loses access the moment IT offboards them
> roles and permissions deeper than "admin" and "everyone else"
> checks that stop user A from reading user B's data by changing one number in the URL
> tenant isolation, so one customer's bug never shows another customer's records
> an admin "log in as this user" button for support, with an audit trail on every use
> rate limits on login, so nobody can guess passwords at scale
> lockouts that stop attackers without locking out your CFO the night before the board meeting
> database migrations that run forward and roll back
> migrations that don't lock the main table at 2pm on a Tuesday
> indexes, because the query that was instant on 50 test rows times out on 5 million real ones
> connection pooling, so a traffic spike doesn't exhaust the database
> backups every night
> a restore from those backups, tested, because a backup you've never restored is a hope
> point-in-time recovery for the day someone runs a delete without a where clause
> soft deletes, so "I deleted it by accident" is a support ticket and not an incident
> validation on the server, not just in the form
> timezones stored right, so the 9am reminder doesn't fire at 4am
> the customer with an apostrophe in their last name
> emoji, accents and right-to-left text in every field
> money stored as integers, because 0.1 + 0.2 doesn't equal 0.3 in floating point
> currency, rounding and tax rules for every country you sell into
> a data model that survives your second customer asking for "one small change"
> idempotency keys, so a retried payment doesn't charge the card twice
> deduplication for the user who clicks submit four times
> pagination that still works on page 400
> exports, because sooner or later every customer wants their data in a spreadsheet
> imports that survive the CSV someone saved in 2009
> retention rules, and code that deletes what your contract says you'll delete
> secrets out of the code, out of the repo and out of the AI chat history
> rotating every key the AI pasted into a config file last month
> confirming every package the AI installed exists and is the one you meant
> dependency scanning, because the AI pulled in libraries nobody reviewed
> input sanitization everywhere a user can type
> protection against SQL injection, XSS, CSRF and the rest of the OWASP list
> file uploads that get scanned, size-limited and stored where they can't execute
> CORS rules that aren't "allow everything"
> security headers on every response
> encryption at rest and in transit
> least-privilege access for everyone, including the AI agent holding production credentials
> logs that record who did what, without recording passwords, tokens or card numbers
> a penetration test before your enterprise customer's security team runs their own
> answers to the security questionnaire every enterprise buyer sends, with evidence behind each one
> a disclosure process for the day a stranger emails you a vulnerability
> a plan for the day a laptop with production access gets stolen
> SOC 2, which means policies, evidence and an auditor, not a checkbox
> HIPAA, the moment a single patient record touches your system
> a BAA with every vendor that touches that data, including your AI model provider
> audit trails that show who viewed a record, not just who changed it
> PCI scope, and card numbers kept out of your database
> GDPR deletion requests that reach every table, backup and log
> data residency for the customer whose contract says EU only
> quarterly access reviews someone signs off on
> dev, staging and production environments that match each other
> infrastructure written as code, so the setup lives somewhere other than one person's memory
> a deploy pipeline that runs the tests before anything reaches customers
> one-click rollbacks, because Friday deploys happen
> zero-downtime deploys, because your customers don't have maintenance windows
> feature flags, so you can ship the code without shipping the feature
> autoscaling for the Monday morning spike
> a CDN, so the app loads fast in Singapore too
> DNS, SSL certificates, and renewals that don't expire on a Sunday
> background job queues, so slow work doesn't freeze the page
> retries with backoff, so one flaky API call doesn't become a lost order
> a dead-letter queue for the jobs that fail every retry
> cron jobs that don't run twice the day you add a second server
> caching, and clearing that cache when the data changes
> SPF, DKIM and DMARC, so your password resets don't land in spam
> bounce and complaint handling on every transactional email
> storage rules, so you stop paying to keep 2021's temp files
> cost alerts, so a runaway agent loop shows up the same day and not on the invoice (we learned this one for $1,382.59)
> a disaster recovery plan, written down and tested once a year
> a second region, if your contract promises uptime one region can't deliver
> structured logs you can search at 3am
> error tracking that groups the same bug instead of sending you 4,000 emails
> uptime checks from outside your own network
> alerts that page a human, tuned until they stop paging for nothing
> dashboards for latency, error rate and throughput
> tracing for one slow request across every service it touches
> an on-call rotation, and a person who picks up
> runbooks, so the engineer on call knows what "queue depth critical" means
> postmortems that change something
> a status page customers check before they email you
> unit tests written by someone who knows what the logic should do
> integration tests for every third-party API you depend on
> end-to-end tests for signup, checkout and the other flows that make you money
> load testing before the launch email goes out
> test data that looks like production without being production data
> regression tests, so fixing bug 41 doesn't bring back bug 12
> testing on the five-year-old laptop your biggest customer's ops team still uses
> accessibility compliance, because the enterprise contract requires it
> subscriptions, upgrades, downgrades and proration
> failed-payment retries and dunning emails
> invoices with the customer's PO number on them, because procurement won't pay without it
> sales tax and VAT
> refunds, credits and partial refunds
> usage metering that matches what you bill, to the cent
> annual contracts with custom terms your billing logic never planned for
> revenue reports your finance team can reconcile
> webhooks that verify signatures
> webhooks that retry, with a log of every failed delivery
> a versioned API, so you can change it without breaking your customers' integrations
> API keys customers can create and revoke
> API rate limits that protect you without blocking real integrations
> a plan for the day a third-party API changes its response format without telling you
> OAuth token refresh, because tokens expire at the worst possible moment
> a sandbox where customers can test their integration
> protection against prompt injection in every field that reaches the model
> customer and patient data kept out of prompts that leave your network
> a model spend cap per customer, so one heavy user can't run up your bill
> evals, so you find out when a model update makes your answers worse
> a fallback for the afternoon your model provider goes down
> a migration plan for the day your model gets deprecated
> prompt and output logs for debugging, minus whatever you're not allowed to keep
> a human approval step for anything the AI does that can't be undone
> pages that load on hotel wifi
> empty states, loading states and error states on every screen
> error messages a customer can act on, instead of "something went wrong"
> forms that keep what people typed when one field fails validation
> emails that render in every mail client your customers use
> notifications people can turn off
> undo
> keyboard navigation and screen reader support
> translations, with dates and numbers formatted for each locale
> a back button that does what people expect
> code a human can read
> code review on every change
> a branching strategy, so two people can work without overwriting each other
> monthly dependency upgrades, so you're never two major versions behind
> framework upgrades before the old version stops getting security patches
> deleting the dead code the AI left behind from its first three attempts
> splitting up the 2,000-line file the AI kept appending to
> architecture decisions written down, with the reasons
> a README that gets a new engineer running locally in under an hour
> documentation for whoever inherits this
> an admin panel for your ops team
> support tooling, so customer success can answer questions without pinging engineering
> a changelog customers can read
> terms and a privacy policy that match what the code does
> every account, domain and repo in the company's name, not the name of whoever built the prototype
> a bus factor higher than one

Oh, and besides keeping all of this working every day, forever… your vibe-coded app will still need people who know what they're doing:

> reading every line the AI wrote before it ships (a senior engineer)
> designing the data model before your second customer breaks it (a backend engineer)
> explaining why the AI's fix for one bug created two new ones (a senior engineer, again)
> deploys, rollbacks, servers and the cloud bill (a DevOps engineer)
> answering the page at 3am when payments stop (whoever's on call)
> patching the framework the week a vulnerability goes public (security)
> walking an auditor through how patient data moves (security and compliance)

text:
A guy was about to tap "Buy Now" on a $299.99 espresso machine on Amazon. Full price.

His wife, a former Amazon fulfillment operations lead, took the phone out of his hands.

She scrolled 3 inches down the exact same product page. Tapped one small gray link. Same machine. Same brand. Same model. Shipped from the same Amazon warehouse. $164.19.

"How?"

"Look at the fulfillment tag. See where it says Amazon Resale: Like New? That means the outer cardboard box got dented on a delivery pallet. The $299.99 is the standard retail listing. The $164.19 is the exact same unopened machine inside a bruised box. Same return protection. Same two-day Prime truck. $135 difference. Because you only look at the yellow Buy Now button."

He looked at her.

"How long have you known this?"

"Since my first week at the fulfillment center. 5 years ago. Everything on Amazon runs on warehouse codes and pricing triggers. LPN stickers track returns. The 15th of the month forces sellers into liquidation. A simple URL code unlocks hidden 70% clearance. I've been using them for years. You've been paying retail for years."

Here's every hidden Amazon warehouse code and pricing rule and what it means for your wallet:

Code 1: "Used - Like New" under Amazon Resale. Brand new products trapped in dented cardboard at up to 40% off retail.

She said this is the single biggest pricing loophole on the entire platform, because most shoppers see the word "Used" and immediately scroll past it.

"Right below the yellow 'Buy Now' button on millions of items, there is a small box that says 'Save with Used - Like New' sold by Amazon Resale, formerly called Amazon Warehouse. Most buyers assume someone used the product at home and sent it back dirty. In the vast majority of cases for 'Like New' grade, that's completely false."

"Inside an Amazon fulfillment center, strict platform compliance rules dictate what can be sold as 'New.' If a forklift bumps a pallet and crushes the corner of a cardboard box, that item is dead as 'New' inventory. If a customer orders the wrong color, opens the outer shipping tape, sees their mistake, and drops it at UPS without ever touching the product inside, it cannot go back into the 'New' bin."

"Instead, a warehouse associate runs a quick visual grading check, sees the factory plastic seal is still intact, grades it 'Used - Like New,' and the pricing system automatically slashes the price by 25% to 50% to clear the shelf space."

"She said 'Used - Like New' and 'Used - Very Good' are how employees furnish their entire homes. 'When I worked the grading station, I watched brand-new $400 kitchen appliances, Sony headphones, and power tools get marked down by $150 simply because the cardboard box had a tear from a box cutter. The machine inside had never been plugged into a wall. Shoppers who click the yellow button pay an extra $135 just to have unwrinkled cardboard that they throw in the recycling bin ten minutes after delivery.'"

Code 2: The "LPN" Barcode Sticker. The warehouse License Plate Number that gives you instant leverage when a "New" item isn't new.

She said this three-letter code is printed on a small white sticker on millions of packages, and knowing what it means gives you immediate leverage with customer support.

"Every single item that passes through an Amazon return center gets slapped with a white barcode sticker starting with the letters 'LPN,' which stands for License Plate Number. That sticker ties the physical box to a specific return ID in Amazon's internal database, recording the return history of that exact unit."

"Here is why you need to check every box you order: fulfillment center workers move fast under intense hourly quotas. Mistakes happen constantly. A returned item with an LPN sticker occasionally gets routed back into the 'New' inventory bin by mistake."

"If you pay full retail price for a 'New' item and it arrives with a white LPN barcode sticker stuck over the original manufacturer barcode, you did not receive untouched factory inventory. You paid full price for a previously returned unit."

"When this happens, you don't have to pack it up and drive to UPS. Open the Amazon customer chat and use the exact warehouse terminology. Tell the agent: 'I paid full retail price for a New item, but the package arrived with an LPN return sticker on the box. Since I received previously returned inventory, I would like an open-box partial credit adjustment to keep it instead of returning it.'"

"She said mentioning the LPN code changes the chat conversation immediately. 'The moment you point out the LPN sticker, the support rep knows a fulfillment grading error happened. Because it costs Amazon money to ship that item back and re-grade it, support agents can offer a partial refund or promotional credit on the spot so you keep the item without triggering a return.'"

Statement : SBI has told the stock exchanges about its data breach, but not the customers whose data was leaked

New Delhi, 21 October 2026

Today, the State Bank of India told the BSE and the National Stock Exchange, in a disclosure under Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, that it has experienced an incident involving the loss of customer data. On 16 October 2026 the bank received alerts from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defence Cyber Agency and CERT-In that its customers’ data was available on the dark web. Its preliminary analysis of about 3.75 lakh records found 3,897 customer records containing personal information. These include registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs and details linked to loan records. The bank says it does not yet know where the data came from, and it has engaged a CERT-In empanelled agency to find out.

SBI did not detect this breach itself and learnt of it from outside agencies after the data had already been published. On the same day, a threat monitoring account on X flagged a claim by a group calling itself “Siriusim” that it had released 3.75 lakh rows of SBI data and 2,722 PDF documents, including loan applications and account opening forms. The bank’s disclosure does not mention these documents. It also does not say what the remaining records, beyond the 3,897 it has identified, contain.

At the time of this statement, SBI has not said that it has informed any of the affected customers, and its disclosure is silent on the point. Five days passed between the alert and today’s filing. The filing assures investors that the incident has no material impact on the bank’s operations, financial performance or business continuity. However, it does not state anything to the 3,897 people whose phone numbers, dates of birth and home addresses are now with fraudsters. These customers are the most likely to receive calls from persons posing as SBI officials who can recite their account details back to them. A customer cannot guard against a fraud she has not been warned of.

The Internet Freedom Foundation calls on SBI to inform every affected customer directly and without further delay.

We regret to note that the law in force today does not compel the bank to do so. Section 8(6) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 requires a Data Fiduciary to intimate a personal data breach to the Data Protection Board and to each affected Data Principal, and Rule 7 of the DPDP Rules, 2025 prescribes how this is to be done. But the Union Government chose a staggered commencement, and these provisions will take effect only on 13 May 2027, nearly four years after Parliament enacted the law. The reporting obligations that apply today, under the CERT-In Directions of 28 April 2022 and the RBI’s cyber security framework for banks, are owed to regulators and not to customers. A listed bank is bound to keep the stock exchanges informed. No law in force clearly binds it to inform the people whose data it holds.

Our demands

1. SBI must inform each affected customer by SMS, email and letter to the registered address, in English, Hindi and the language of the customer’s branch, stating what data was exposed and what steps they should take. It should open a dedicated helpline and an online facility for customers to check whether their data is affected.

2. SBI must state what the 3.75 lakh records and the 2,722 documents contain, how many customers they relate to, and whether they include KYC documents such as Aadhaar, PAN or passport copies.

3. When the investigation concludes, SBI must disclose how the data left its systems, including whether it came through a vendor or a direct selling agent, and publish a summary of the investigating agency’s findings.

4. The Reserve Bank of India should direct all regulated entities to notify customers of personal data breaches within a fixed period, pending the commencement of the DPDP Act.

5. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology should bring Section 8(6) of the DPDP Act and Rule 7 of the DPDP Rules into force immediately.

IEC enters into partnership to counter disinformation | @SAgovnews

October 20, 2026

The Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) has entered into a partnership with Google, Meta, Microsoft, TikTok and non-profit organisation, Moxii Africa, to ensure the integrity of election information and counter disinformation ahead of the 4 November 2026 Local Government Elections.

The partnership is a sequel to a similar framework signed with the platforms ahead of the 2024 National and Provincial Elections (NPE). It is an indispensable lever buttressing the Commission’s purposive measures to enhance the integrity of election information.

These measures include the gazetting of the Electoral Code of Conduct Countering Disinformation in the Local Government Elections (the Disinformation Code), on 4 September 2026.

The Code applies to political parties, candidates and anyone acting on their behalf. It forms part of the Electoral Code of Conduct and carries the same sanctions. 

According to the Commission, the partnership brings the platforms into the same effort to keep election information accurate and trustworthy.

Underscoring the importance of the partnership, the Commission’s Chief Electoral Officer Sy Mamabolo said the strategic inclusion of the online platforms gives the Commission direct access to the platforms and a real fighting chance against disinformation.

“Our partnership with digital platforms is critical to ensuring that voters have access to credible, accurate and trustworthy information to make informed political choices. A technically flawless election can still lose public trust if citizens are overwhelmed by disinformation.

“Therefore, the partnership eliminates barriers to direct access to the platforms and enables instantaneous remedial action against disinformation peddlers,” Mamabolo said.

The partnership covers the following:
• Cooperation in good faith during the election period;
• Respect for existing laws, with no requirement to share confidential user data;
• Alignment with the Constitution, municipal electoral laws and the Electoral Code of Conduct, including the Disinformation Code;
• A working group of partners, election awareness campaigns, and training on disinformation for political parties, candidates and other stakeholders;
• Room for platforms to apply their own policies, including content removal, advisory warnings and delisting, and
• Cooperation on other initiatives intended to curb the impact of disinformation in elections.
 The Commission has designated the Real411 platform to support its proactive efforts to minimise the impact of disinformation during the 2026 Local Government Elections.

Anyone who sees suspected election-related disinformation can report it to Real411 at https://t.co/Kc7kXVrgbE or through the Real411 app.

Complaints are handled in all eleven official languages. Real411 assesses complaints independently and recommends action to the Commission and the platforms.

Depending on the findings, the Commission, upon careful review of any reported complaint indicating disinformation or misinformation, can: 
• Refer the matter to the Electoral Court, which can impose sanctions. 
• Promptly refer the matter to the relevant online platform, which is expected to prioritise referrals from the Commission by acknowledging and swiftly processing the notification in line with its policies. 
• Issue media statements to alert the public and correct the disinformation. Guidance for voters on spotting, checking and reporting disinformation is available at https://t.co/7XX2mAKHXp.

The partners welcomed the partnership and reaffirmed their commitment to working with the Commission. They noted that they already have policies and mechanisms to counter disinformation and will keep using them as part of the collective effort.

“Free, fair and credible elections depend on people being able to trust the information they see. No single organisation can tackle disinformation alone, which is why Microsoft is pleased to join the Electoral Commission in this partnership.

“Ahead of the 2026 Local Government Elections, we will work alongside the Commission, civil society and industry to help voters find authoritative election information, strengthen media and AI literacy, and counter deceptive AI-generated content,” said Director: Government Affairs, Microsoft South Africa, Abongile Vanda in affirming Microsoft’s support for the partnership.

“At TikTok, we recognise the important role our platform plays in helping people discover information and engage in public conversations. This is why we take our responsibility to protect our community during elections very seriously.

“Through our in-app Election Centre, South Africans will be able to access reliable information about the elections, and to further support this, we have introduced election-related labels and search banners that direct users to the centre with a single tap.

“This work is supported by advanced moderation, collaboration with fact-checking partners and electoral commissions like the IEC South Africa to ensure a safe, informed, and authentic election experience for our community,” TikTok’s Government Relations and Public Policy Lead for Southern Africa, Tholoana Ncheke-Mahlaela, said.

“Information integrity is fundamental to the credibility of any democratic process. In an increasingly complex digital environment, protecting voters from misinformation and disinformation requires coordinated action across institutions, technology platforms, civil society and citizens themselves.

“This partnership represents an important commitment to ensuring that South Africans can access accurate, trustworthy election information and participate in the 2026 Local Government Elections with confidence,” Moxii Africa Director William Bird welcoming the partnership.

Bird said he is proud to support this collective effort to strengthen trust, transparency and democratic resilience.

text:
Starlink has an Indian license, 20 ground stations on Indian soil, and a promise to keep Indian user data in India. What it doesn't have is permission to switch on.

Thousands of Indian villages still have no 4G. In the Northeast alone, more than 1,800 had no mobile signal of any kind as of February, most of them in Arunachal Pradesh. These are the places satellite internet is built for: mountain villages, islands, flood zones, anywhere a tower or a fiber line takes years and a lot of money to arrive.

Starlink has done what India asked. It got its telecom license in June 2025 and space regulator approval a month later. It built India-specific security controls, agreed to keep data local, and has been reporting the names, addresses and coordinates of its test terminals to the government every two weeks. It operates in more than 150 countries. In India it still can't sell a single subscription, and the company is now talking about early 2027.

New Delhi says nobody is being singled out, since Eutelsat OneWeb and Jio's satellite venture are stuck at the same stage. I believe that, and I don't think it helps. When three licensed operators, two of them backed by India's biggest telecom groups, can't clear security review after more than a year of trials, that tells you the process has no deadline. It doesn't tell you it's thorough.

The security concerns are real. Indian agencies have been rattled by smuggled terminals turning up in border areas, and India is entitled to lawful interception, local data storage and an emergency shutoff. Starlink has already signed up for all of it. The answer to a misused terminal is enforcement, not keeping the service dark for everyone who would use it legally.

Elon Musk has been blunt, calling the delay "a crime against the people of India" and asking, "Is Ambani the real boss of India?" You don't need to buy the whole oligarch theory to see his point. Reliance spent months lobbying for spectrum auctions that would have favored deep-pocketed incumbents. The government sided with Starlink on that one, which is to its credit. Now it needs to finish the job.

India can keep every security power it wants and still let a kid in Arunachal get online. Right now it's choosing not to.
